---
title: "Calling the emulator"
---
















Two calls stand between covariates and a trajectory. One fetches a checkpoint from Hugging
Face, the other runs it over a list of scenarios.

## Loading a checkpoint

::: {#ffdfacd1 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

prevalence = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

print(type(prevalence).__name__)
print(prevalence.model_config["predictor"])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
ModelArtifact
prevalence
```
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note}
## The return type

The classmethod hangs off `Mamba2Regressor`, but what it hands back is a `ModelArtifact`. It
is a container holding the network (`.model`), its architecture (`.model_config`), the input
recipe (`.preprocessing_config`) and the fitted covariate scaler (`.scaler`). You call
`.predict` on the artifact, not the network. The network on its own would not know how
to scale your covariates.
:::

`predictor` selects which of the two checkpoints in the repository to fetch. The two are
separately trained networks with separately fitted scalers. The scalers are not
interchangeable.

::: {#4c1322e7 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

cases = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="cases", revision="v1.2.2",
)

print("same scaler means:", np.allclose(prevalence.scaler.mean_, cases.scaler.mean_))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
same scaler means: False
```
:::
:::


Load the artifact that matches the quantity you want. Running covariates through the
prevalence artifact and reading the result as case counts raises no error at all, and the
scaling applied to them is wrong.

## Predicting

`.predict` takes a **list of dicts**, one dict per scenario. It returns a `(B, 157)` array,
one row per scenario and one column per fortnightly window.

::: {#b1f5ff5c .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
district = {
    "eir": 31.96,          # from estiMINT, for a measured prevalence of 0.45
    "dn0_use": 0.311,      # pyrethroid-only nets at 30% resistance
    "Q0": 0.85,
    "phi_bednets": 0.80,
    "seasonal": 0,
    "routine": 0.0,
    "itn_use": 0.70,
    "irs_use": 0.0,
    "dn0_future": 0.485,   # switch to PBO
    "itn_future": 0.70,    # same coverage sustained
    "irs_future": 0.0,
    "lsm": 0.0,
}

y = prevalence.predict([district])
print(y.shape)
print(f"prevalence at the campaign: {y[0, 78]:.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
(1, 157)
prevalence at the campaign: 0.456
```
:::
:::


Column 78 is the window the campaign lands in.
[Covariates and the time grid](covariates.qmd) derives that index from the checkpoint rather
than assuming it. The value there is close to the prevalence given to estiMINT (0.45).

A single scenario is still a list of one. It still comes back with a leading batch
dimension. Three scenarios come back stacked.

::: {#f9f23fe0 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
campaigns = [
    dict(district, dn0_future=0.0,   itn_future=0.0),   # nets withdrawn
    dict(district, dn0_future=0.311, itn_future=0.70),  # like-for-like pyrethroid
    dict(district, dn0_future=0.485, itn_future=0.70),  # switch to PBO
]

Y = prevalence.predict(campaigns)
print(Y.shape)
print(np.round(Y[:, -1], 3))   # prevalence three years on
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
(3, 157)
[0.498 0.484 0.47 ]
```
:::
:::


The rows come back in the order you supplied them. The mapping from scenario to row is yours
to keep track of.

## Transformed space

The networks are trained on transformed targets, a logit for prevalence and a `log1p` for
cases. By default `.predict` inverts the transform and gives you the quantity itself.
`transformed=True` suppresses the inversion.

::: {#fbb48fe2 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
raw = prevalence.predict([district], transformed=True)
inv = prevalence.predict([district])

print("logit space  :", np.round(raw[0, :3], 3))
print("prevalence   :", np.round(inv[0, :3], 3))
print("sigmoid(raw) :", np.round(1 / (1 + np.exp(-raw[0, :3])), 3))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
logit space  : [-0.203 -0.197 -0.248]
prevalence   : [0.449 0.451 0.438]
sigmoid(raw) : [0.449 0.451 0.438]
```
:::
:::


The default is what you want unless you are scoring the model against a held-out set in the
space it was trained in.

## Negative case counts

The inverse of `log1p` is `expm1`, so a prediction slightly below zero in log space becomes
a case count slightly below zero. The magnitude is a fraction of a case. Under a strong
campaign, where true incidence is close to the floor, it happens often.

::: {#519429ed .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
aggressive = dict(
    district, dn0_future=0.55, itn_future=0.95, irs_future=0.90, lsm=0.90,
)

c = cases.predict([aggressive])
print(f"minimum        : {c.min():.4f}")
print(f"negative steps : {int((c < 0).sum())} of {c.shape[1]}")

c = np.maximum(c, 0.0)
print(f"after flooring : {c.min():.4f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
minimum        : -0.0232
negative steps : 59 of 157
after flooring : 0.0000
```
:::
:::


Floor the case trajectory with `np.maximum` before you plot it or sum it.
[`run_scenarios`](../06-scenarios/run-scenarios.qmd) applies exactly this floor, so results
that come out of the pipeline are already clean. Results that come straight out of a
checkpoint are not.

Prevalence needs no such treatment. A logit inverts through a sigmoid, and a sigmoid cannot
leave `[0, 1]`.

## The raw feature matrix

`.prepare_inputs` runs the first half of `.predict` and stops. It expands your twelve
covariates onto the time grid, masks the campaign fields before day 3285, scales everything
and appends the time features. What comes back is the tensor the network actually consumes.

::: {#caeec314 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
X = prevalence.prepare_inputs(campaigns)
print(X.shape, X.dtype)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
(3, 157, 16) float32
```
:::
:::


There are sixteen channels, the twelve scaled covariates plus four time features that locate
each window in the year and relative to the campaign. Use it to confirm that the campaign
masking is doing what you think. A normal analysis has no need of it. The layout is set out
in [stateMINT internals](../07-under-the-hood/statemint-internals.qmd).

## Pinning the revision

`revision` is optional and defaults to `main`, which moves. A re-run of an unpinned analysis
several months from now may not be running the same weights it ran today. The published tags
run from `v1.0.0` to `v1.2.2`. Pass one of them explicitly.

```python
Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained("dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="cases", revision="v1.2.2")
```
